topics: 🏠 Covered Domains — why Rebbi's rule works for a covered private domain but not a covered public one
🎯 Acherim's Baraita — a thrower is liable only if the catcher stands still, not if he runs for it
🖐 A Hand Worth Four by Four — Rava and Rabbi Yochanan's principle cuts through a tangle of forced readings
💧 Water on Water — when gathering rainwater counts as a valid act of lifting
🚶 Carrying All Day Without Stopping — liability begins only once a person comes to rest

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Covered Domains, a Hand's Worth, and a Drop of Rain
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 5a–5b
overview.hebrewSource: יָדוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם חֲשׁוּבָה לוֹ כְּאַרְבָּעָה עַל אַרְבָּעָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Daf 5 continues hunting for the source behind the mishna's liability for a hand too small to meet the usual four-by-four-handbreadth requirement. After testing and rejecting an explanation based on covered domains, the Gemara turns to a baraita of Acherim about someone who catches a thrown object, then works through several increasingly technical proposals — a basket, a lowered hand, a short person — before Rava and, independently, Rabbi Yochanan cut through the tangle with a simple principle: a person's hand is significant enough, on its own, to count as four by four handbreadths. The daf then applies related reasoning to gathering rainwater, a floating nut, and oil on wine, before turning to the separate question of when a person carrying an object all day is considered to have made a halakhic placement at all.

slides.title: 🏠 Covered Domains — A Rule That Doesn't Travel
slides.subtitle: Rebbi's liability for a covered private domain cannot be stretched to a covered public one
rows: Liable, even without a defined landing spot
בֵּיתָא כְּמַאן דְּמַלְיָא דָּמְיָא — the house is considered as though filled; anything passing through it is as if it landed on solid ground
Without a roof, there is no basis to treat the airspace as 'filled'
Not liable (a separate ruling of Rav)
Carrying four cubits there is exempt, because a covered public domain is unlike the desert encampment on which the melakha of carrying is modeled

callout.label: Why this fails:
callout.text: Since even Rebbi's own reasoning cannot extend from a covered private domain to a covered public one, a covered roof cannot be the true explanation for our mishna's liability.

slides.title: 🎯 Acherim: It Depends on the Catcher, Not Just the Thrower
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Zeira finds a different tannaitic source for the mishna

nodes.content: ❓ If a covered domain isn't the answer, whose opinion explains our mishna's liability for a mere hand?
💡 Rabbi Zeira: it is the opinion of אֲחֵרִים (Acherim), from a baraita about one who catches a thrown object

columns.label: Stood still and caught it
columns.content: The thrower is LIABLE — his own lifting, combined with the catcher's stillness, completes the act

columns.label: Ran toward it and caught it
columns.content: The thrower is EXEMPT — the catcher's own movement, not the thrower's act, brought the object to rest

nodes.content: ✅ Since Acherim impose liability even though the receiving hand has no 4×4 surface, they too require no defined area for placing

callout.label: Not airtight:
callout.text: The Gemara immediately questions the proof: perhaps only placing needs no 4×4 for Acherim, while lifting still does; or perhaps the catcher extended the folds of his cloak, which does provide 4×4.

slides.title: 🖐 A Person's Hand Is Worth Four by Four
slides.subtitle: A tangle of forced readings, cut through by one simple principle

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Abba first tries: the mishna really means a basket (טְרַסְקָל) in hand, not the bare hand — but the mishna's own words say 'his hand,' not 'a basket'

2️⃣ Rabbi Abbahu tries instead: the poor person lowered his hand below three handbreadths off the ground, where the principle of lavud makes it 'as good as touching the ground' — forcing the mishna's word 'stands' to mean 'bends,' 'in a pit,' or 'a very short person'
3️⃣ Rava objects: would the tanna really go to all this trouble rather than simply state the halakha?

4️⃣ Rava's principle — echoed independently by Rabbi Yochanan: יָדוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם חֲשׁוּבָה לוֹ כְּאַרְבָּעָה עַל אַרְבָּעָה — a person's hand is significant enough, on its own, to count as four by four handbreadths

callout.label: Extended further:
callout.text: Rabbi Yochanan adds: even if the object lands in ANOTHER person's hand without his intending to catch it, the hand's significance still applies — it does not depend on the receiver having deemed his own hand significant.

slides.title: 💧 Water on Water, and a Floating Nut
slides.subtitle: Applying the same logic of 'has it come to rest?' to gathering rainwater

boxes.title: Gathered off a Sloped Wall
items: Works for a rolling SCROLL — a book naturally settles against an incline
Fails for WATER — water never truly rests on a slope; it keeps flowing

boxes.title: Gathered off a Water-Filled Hole
items: Succeeds: water already sitting in a hole has come to rest
Rava's principle: מַיִם עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם הַיְינוּ הַנָּחָתָן — water on top of water IS its own placement

boxes.title: A Floating Nut
items: A nut floating on water is NOT considered placed — it drifts
Rava's dilemma: a nut inside a floating VESSEL — follow the nut (at rest) or the vessel (still moving)? Unresolved — teiku

callout.label: Same test elsewhere:
callout.text: The Gemara notes a parallel dispute over oil floating on wine — whether the two are considered connected — which likewise turns on this question of what counts as truly 'at rest.'

slides.title: 🚶 Carrying All Day Without Stopping
slides.subtitle: When does a person laden with objects make a halakhic 'placement'?

lines.speaker: R' Yochanan
lines.text: One laden with food and drink who enters and exits a domain all day long is not liable by Torah law — not until he stands still.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: And that is specifically if he stopped in order to rest. If he merely paused to adjust the burden on his shoulder, that does not count as a placement.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Proof: the same distinction applies to carrying four cubits in the public domain — stopping to rest exempts him mid-way, but stopping to shift his load does not.

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: One who carries an object from a store to a plaza via a colonnade is liable — yet ben Azzai exempts him, holding that walking itself counts as coming to rest at every single step.

callout.label: Left open:
callout.text: The Rabbis, unlike ben Azzai, hold that walking is not like standing — so how can passing through the colonnade, an exempt domain, ever produce liability? The daf ends without an answer; it is taken up on daf 6.

summary.principle: The mishna's liability for a hand too small to be four by four handbreadths is explained by the principle that a person's hand is itself significant enough to count as that area — and the same test of 'has it truly come to rest?' governs whether gathering rainwater, or carrying an object all day without stopping, constitutes a halakhic placement.

flowSteps.content: 🏠 Covered private domain works for Rebbi's liability rule; covered public domain does not
🎯 Rabbi Zeira: Acherim's baraita — thrower liable only if the catcher stands still, not if he runs to catch it
🖐 Rava & Rabbi Yochanan: a person's hand is significant enough to count as 4×4 handbreadths on its own

columns.content: 💧 Water on water IS a placement; a floating nut is not
🚶 Carrying all day isn't liable until one stops to REST, not merely to adjust a load

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: liability turns on whether an object has truly come to rest — and a person's own hand always counts as a defined place

quiz.q: According to Rebbi, in which type of domain is one liable for an object that merely passes through without landing on a defined four-by-four surface?
o: Any public domain
A covered private domain, because the house is considered as though filled
A karmelit
An uncovered private domain
quiz.e: Rebbi's rule is בֵּיתָא כְּמַאן דְּמַלְיָא — a covered house is treated as filled space, so anything passing through it is as if it landed on solid ground. He does not extend this to an uncovered domain.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject extending Rebbi's 'covered domain' reasoning to a covered PUBLIC domain?
o: Because public domains cannot have roofs
Because Rav ruled that carrying four cubits in a covered public domain is exempt, since it is unlike the desert encampment
Because covered domains are always private
Because the mishna never mentions a public domain
quiz.e: Rav's ruling that a covered public domain does not create liability for carrying shows that 'covered' cannot be the operative factor behind the mishna.

quiz.q: According to the baraita of Acherim, when is one who throws an object liable for another person catching it?
o: Only if the catcher is a priest
Only if the catcher stands still and receives it; if he runs toward it, the thrower is exempt
Only if the object is food
Never — the catcher is always liable instead
quiz.e: Acherim rule that the thrower is liable if the catcher stood in place and received the object, but exempt if the catcher moved from his place to catch it, since then the catcher's own motion completed the placement.

quiz.q: What does the principle יָדוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם חֲשׁוּבָה לוֹ כְּאַרְבָּעָה עַל אַרְבָּעָה establish?
o: That a hand may never be used to carry objects on Shabbat
That a person's own hand is significant enough to count as an area of four by four handbreadths for lifting and placing
That priests' hands are more significant than other people's
That only the right hand counts for halakhic purposes
quiz.e: Rava, and independently Rabbi Yochanan, taught that a person's hand itself has the halakhic status of a defined four-by-four space, resolving the mishna's liability without needing baskets or bent knees.

quiz.q: Why does gathering rainwater from atop a water-filled hole count as a valid act of lifting, while scooping a floating nut off open water does not?
o: Because water is heavier than a nut
Because water on top of water is considered its own placement, while a floating nut has not come to rest
Because nuts are never subject to Shabbat prohibitions
Because holes are always private domains
quiz.e: Rava's principle is מַיִם עַל גַּבֵּי מַיִם הַיְינוּ הַנָּחָתָן — water resting on water counts as placed — whereas a nut floating on water keeps moving and has not achieved a halakhic placement.
